paras: The threatened lynching of Major Lee took place at Moultrie, Georgia, in August 1903, when a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a young white girl was moved out of the Moultrie jail because a lynching had been arranged for him. Sheriff Murphy of Colquitt County sent him by train to the Thomasville jail, and no attack on him was reported. Dispatches from Moultrie gave the prisoner's name as Major Alexander.

According to a Thomasville dispatch dated August 11, Lee was accused of attempting to assault the 14-year-old daughter of a Mr. Shaw near Moultrie that morning, and was caught soon after and jailed at Moultrie. The Moultrie correspondents told a fuller version: a girl of 13, walking home from town with a young brother, saw a man crouch in the bushes ahead of her and called to men in a nearby field. The men found him hiding, and he ran but was caught and brought to the Moultrie jail.

Sheriff Murphy learned that a "lynching bee" had been arranged for the night of August 11. He took the prisoner out of town, stopped a Tifton, Thomasville and Gulf train some distance away, and sent him aboard with Deputy Sheriff Collier to Thomasville, where he arrived late that afternoon. A Moultrie dispatch dated the next day said there had been "some talk of lynching" but that it would "probably be prevented", without mentioning the removal.

At Thomasville, Lee said he was "entirely innocent of the charge", and the correspondent wrote that his explanation "sounds very plausible". No report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the Thomasville dispatch on its front page on August 12 under the headline "MOULTRIE MOB AFTER SUPPOSED NEGRO RAPIST". The same story both credited Lee's explanation and called him "a negro of very shady reputation" who had been jailed several times. A day later the paper's Moultrie column placed the arrest between news of a new mayor and a raid on "blind tigers".

The Atlanta Constitution printed two specials on one page on August 17: a shortened Thomasville item that left out Lee's denial, and a Moultrie item that called the accused "a bad character" fresh from the chain gang. That Moultrie item said the girl "escaped a most terrible fate", treating the charge as established. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.

The two sets of dispatches differ on the accused's surname, Lee or Alexander, and on the girl's age, 14 or 13. They also differ on timing: the Thomasville dispatch has him moved on August 11, while the Moultrie dispatches place his jailing at Moultrie on August 12.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Major Lee
bases: A Thomasville dispatch says a 'lynching bee had been arranged' for a jailed Black prisoner and the sheriff removed him to another town, and a Moultrie dispatch reports 'some talk of lynching' (A1, A2, A4); no attack on him is reported, so this is a threatened lynching.

No one was killed: the prisoner was moved to the Thomasville jail before the planned 'lynching bee' (A1, A4). The planned act had no lawful authority and answered an accusation of attempted assault, but the size of the would-be mob is not given (A1, A2).

A Thomasville dispatch (A1, reprinted as A4) and separate Moultrie dispatches (A2, A3) agree that a Black man named Major was jailed at Moultrie on a charge of attempting to assault a young girl, and A1 and A2 both report lynching talk, though they differ on his surname, the girl's age and the date (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: Thomasville dispatch
accounts.gist: Lee was caught soon after the alleged attempt on Shaw's daughter on the morning of Aug. 11; the sheriff learned of a 'lynching bee' set for that night and sent him by train to Thomasville, where Lee said he was innocent.

accounts.label: Moultrie dispatches
accounts.gist: 'Major Alexander' was jailed at Moultrie on Aug. 12 after a 13-year-old girl called to men in a field, who found him hiding in bushes and caught him as he ran; one dispatch adds that lynching talk would 'probably be prevented'.

accounts.label: The accused
accounts.gist: Lee said he was 'entirely innocent' and the Thomasville writer judged his explanation 'very plausible'.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'MOULTRIE MOB AFTER SUPPOSED NEGRO RAPIST', reported Lee's innocence claim as 'very plausible', yet called him 'a negro of very shady reputation'.
The Savannah Moultrie column reported the arrest between a mayoral election and a liquor raid and forecast that lynching 'will probably be prevented'.

The Atlanta Constitution's Moultrie special called the accused 'a bad character' and said the girl 'escaped a most terrible fate', treating the charge as fact; its Thomasville special dropped the innocence claim.

conflicts.note: Same first name, town, charge and week; the Thomasville dispatch is the only one naming the girl's father and reporting the removal.
The Moultrie dispatches name no family.

versions.value: Attempt on the morning of Aug. 11; moved to Thomasville late that afternoon

conflicts.note: The Moultrie dispatches say nothing of the removal; the Aug. 12 one may have been written the day before its dateline, but the coverage does not settle it.

quotes: MOULTRIE MOB AFTER SUPPOSED NEGRO RAPIST.
Major Lee, a negro, was brought to Thomasville late this afternoon from Moultrie to escape lynching.
Sheriff Murphy of Colquitt county, got onto the fact that a lynching bee had been arranged for to-night.
Lee says that he is entirely innocent of the charge, and his explanation of his suspicious actions sounds very plausible.
He is a negro of very shady reputation, having been in jail both here and at Moultrie several times.
